intro: People hit balls with sticks and ran between marks for hundreds of years. In England, children played rounders and stoolball. In American towns, people played town ball. Each place had its own bases, its own distances and its own way to make an out.

In the 1840s and 1850s, clubs in New York wrote their rules down. They set the bases ninety feet apart and a game at nine innings. Writers like Henry Chadwick printed box scores and guides. Leagues, umpires and scorers kept the game the same from town to town.

In this unit you will read old rules, a town law, a legend and a rule book. You will be able to explain how baseball got its measured field. You will also explain how scorebooks let strangers compare games.
bigQuestion: How did written rules and written scores turn a loose game into one baseball that many towns could share?

timeline.t: A Little Pretty Pocket-Book, printed in London, has a page titled Base-Ball
Pittsfield, Massachusetts, bans baseball near its new meeting house
The Knickerbocker Base Ball Club of New York writes its rules
A New York convention sets bases ninety feet apart and games at nine innings
Beadle's Dime Base-Ball Player, edited by Henry Chadwick, is first printed
The Cincinnati Red Stockings become the first openly all-professional team
The National League is founded; Chicago wins its first pennant
The pitching distance is set at 60 feet 6 inches
The IHSA is founded, and home plate becomes a five-sided plate
The Mills Commission reports the Doubleday legend
The National Baseball Hall of Fame opens in Cooperstown
Belleville wins the first Illinois state baseball tournament

words.d: an old English bat-and-ball game in which a hitter runs around a loop of posts
a rule made by a town or a club for its own members or land
a story told as history that cannot be proven and may not be true
a long walking step, once used to measure distance
a meeting where clubs or groups vote on shared rules
a player who is paid to play as a job
a group of teams that play one schedule under one set of rules
the rubber slab that marks the pitching distance, used since 1893
a small table that shows each player's numbers for one game
a judge who watches a game and settles what happened under the rules
the one person who keeps a game's official record and rules on hits and errors
Illinois High School Association, the group that runs school sports in Illinois, founded in 1900

test.q: What does the 1744 book A Little Pretty Pocket-Book show?
choices: an early printed use of the word base-ball
test.why: Newbery's 1744 book has a page titled Base-Ball.

test.q: Why did Pittsfield pass its 1791 bylaw?
choices: to protect its meeting house windows
test.why: The bylaw kept ball games 80 yards from the new meeting house.

test.q: What do historians say about the Doubleday story?
choices: It is proven by many records.
It is a legend with no good evidence.
test.why: The Mills Commission's claim rested on one late letter; historians call it a legend.

test.q: Which club wrote baseball rules in 1845?
test.why: The Knickerbocker club of New York wrote its rules in 1845.

test.q: Why were paces a problem for measuring bases?
choices: Paces were only used in England.
Paces were too short for any field.
test.why: A pace depends on the walker, so fields differed.

choices: ninety feet between bases and nine-inning games
test.why: The 1857 rules set thirty yards between bases and nine innings.

test.q: Which team was the first openly all-professional team?
test.why: Every 1869 Red Stockings player was openly paid.

test.q: Who led the founding of the National League in 1876?
test.why: William Hulbert, who ran the Chicago club, led the plan.

test.q: What was the pitching distance from 1881 to 1892?
test.why: The National League used 50 feet from 1881 until 1893.

choices: a small table of each player's numbers in one game
test.why: Box scores, made common by Chadwick, list each player's numbers.

test.q: Which game's scoring did Chadwick know before baseball?
test.why: Chadwick grew up with English cricket score sheets.

test.q: What does the official scorer decide?
choices: whether a play is a hit or an error
test.why: The scorer records hits and errors; the umpire rules on plays.

test.q: What did the 1845 rules say about the umpire?
choices: There was no appeal from the umpire's decision.
The umpire was paid by the league.
test.why: The Knickerbocker rules made the umpire's decision final.

test.q: Why did the catcher's mask appear in the 1870s?
choices: because catchers moved closer and got hurt
because the Hall of Fame asked
test.why: Catchers moved nearer the batter as pitching got harder.

test.q: When was the first Illinois state baseball tournament held?
test.why: Belleville won the first state baseball tournament in 1940. The IHSA took charge of it in 1941.

write.prompt: Which mattered more for making one baseball that many towns could share: measuring the field, or writing down the score? Use two or three records from this unit, such as the 1845 Knickerbocker rules, the 1857 convention, Beadle's 1860 guide or the Official Baseball Rules.
tips: Name each record and its year.
Say what the record changed for clubs in other towns.
Use unit words such as convention, box score and official scorer.
Call the Doubleday story a legend if you mention it.
End by saying which choice you think mattered more and why.
